name: Leap
summary: On a key, the unit jumps along an arc to a chosen spot within reach, clearing walls, gaps, ledges and other units, and lands a moment later; then the key needs time to recharge, or a small stock of jumps refills one at a time. It lets a unit take high ground, cross terrain that others must walk round, dive onto a target or get out of a fight. Many versions add something to the landing, such as damage and knockback in a small circle, or make the jumper hard to hit while airborne. A line that winches the unit up to a ledge, a passive hop up and down ledges, and a pad that launches anyone who steps on it are variants. A burst of speed along the ground is dash, an instant blink is teleport, and arriving from the sky on a chosen spot is drop-in-from-above.
counterplay: Read the landing: the ring or shadow shows where it will come down, so step away, pre-aim the spot or put a mine or hazard on it.
Punish the recovery: right after landing it needs a moment before it can act, and its jump is then recharging.
Shoot it in the air: mid-jump it follows a fixed arc and can't dodge much.
Root, slow or stun it so it can't jump away when the key comes back.
Hold positions that take more than one jump to reach, and cover the perches it can reach.
Track its cooldown: a jumper whose jump is spent can't escape.

other_examples.note: Jump-pack melee infantry that hop over whatever terrain lies in the way to a targeted spot. Jumps are stored as charges that refill slowly, so a squad can make two jumps in a row and then waits. Players jump them onto enemy ranged specialists, use the mobility for hit-and-run raids on strategic points, and even send them deep inside the enemy base as spotters for artillery or for a deep strike.

sources.title: Soulstorm/Assault Marine Squad, Dawn of War Wiki
Dawn of War/Assault Marine Squad, Dawn of War Wiki

other_examples.note: The squad spends energy to fly to a target spot, and the landing knocks back enemies in a small circle. While airborne the squad shrugs off suppression and takes only a small share of ranged damage; the jump itself recharges almost at once, so energy is the real limit. The campaign's jump pack wargear gives the hero a similar jump whose value lies in crashing down on light infantry.

sources.title: Dawn of War II/Jump (Assault Squad), Dawn of War Wiki
Retribution/Jump (Assault Squad), Dawn of War Wiki
Jump Pack, Dawn of War Wiki

other_examples.note: A passive version: reapers hop up and down cliffs by themselves, one level at a time, with no dropship or spotter, but they can't clear obstacles or force fields. The fast, fragile raider uses cliff edges to hit workers and slip away from melee units that must walk round.

sources.title: Reaper (Legacy of the Void), Liquipedia StarCraft II Wiki
SCAbility/Jet Pack, Liquipedia StarCraft II Wiki

other_examples.note: Heavy railgun infantry with a jetpack ability on a short cooldown: one long hop to a targeted spot over rough ground and obstacles, used to get round terrain or escape a force that would overwhelm them. A Kane's Wrath patch (1.02) dropped a small delay before take-off and made the flight faster.

sources.title: Zone trooper (Tiberium Wars), Command & Conquer Wiki

other_examples.note: Short rocket-powered leaps over obstacles and bad terrain, limited by heat (even a short jump heats a 'Mech more than running) and a few seconds of thrust. A jumping 'Mech is harder to hit but shoots less accurately, a damaged leg can make it fall on landing, and Death From Above lets it land on an enemy to crush it, at the risk of hurting itself.

shooter_analogues.note: A tank's leap forward on a short cooldown: the landing hurts and knocks back nearby enemies, more the closer it lands to them, and he can still fire and steer a little in the air. Bumping into a box or low wall right at take-off cancels it. Players use it to reach snipers on high ground and to dive in and out of fights; his ultimate shortens the cooldown.

Jets give upward thrust for a few seconds, then must recharge, and each use adds heat; they let a 'Mech reach rooftops and take short cuts. Pilots keep a little thrust back to brake, because a hard landing damages the legs, and the poptart tactic pops out of cover upwards, fires and sinks back. Landing on an enemy is not in this game.

A whole class built on jump jets, used to flank from angles others can't reach. Most jet types burn a fuel tank, each balancing climb against distance; the Ambusher type instead gives one strong, mostly forward burst on a cooldown and leaves the trooper exposed until it recharges.

shooter_analogues.unit: Grappling hook (Battlefield 2042 grapple gun, earlier gadgets)
shooter_analogues.note: In 2042 a specialist's grapple gun has unlimited shots on a modest cooldown: it catches most surfaces, reels the player in quickly, pulls them over the ledge it caught on and can hurt infantry it strikes. In Hardline a launcher leaves a rope on a ledge for climbing, one rope per player, which can be shot or cut; Battlefield 2's thrown hook made a rope to scale buildings.

An ultimate that places a pad which flings any player who steps on it through the air, along the way they were already heading, with a double jump to steer; enemies can use it too. It is loud, can be shot, and teams use it to flank over rocks or carry a downed teammate to safety.

The victim's side: jump-pack enemies hop behind players to flank them, but the jets are loud, their landing spot is easy to predict and they can't fire while flying. Players shoot them out of the air with precise rifles, wait under the landing spot, or leave a trip mine where they will come down.

player_translation.summary: A cooldown jump for one player: aim a landing spot within reach, arc over walls, gaps and ledges, and land with a short recovery. Variants add a landing strike, stored jumps, a grapple line or a pad the whole team can use.
as_user: Press Q and you jump to the point under the cursor, clamped to your jump range; a ring shows where you will land before you commit, and you can't land inside walls.
In the air you can steer only a little and, in the base version, can't fire; you land with a short recovery before you can act again.
Use it to take high ground, cross a gap the enemy has to walk round, reach a sniper's perch or get out of a losing fight.
The cooldown makes every jump a decision: jump in, and you may not be able to jump out.
With the landing strike, coming down in a group knocks them back and hurts them; with stored jumps you can chain two.
as_target: You see the jumper's landing ring and a growing shadow a moment before it lands, so you can step away, pre-aim, or put a mine or hazard on the spot.
While airborne it counts as a low flier: anything that reaches low air can hit it, but ground effects such as mines and zones don't catch it until it lands.
After it lands it has a short recovery: that is your window.
Watch its jump cooldown: a jumper whose jump is spent can't escape.
teammates: A jumper scouts high ground and ledges for its team and pings what it sees.
It opens fights: a landing strike in a group knocks enemies about for teammates to finish.
The launch-pad variant lets the whole team use the route it opens.
The other team covers likely landing spots together with mines, hazards and roots.
controls: Move with WASD and aim with the mouse; left mouse fires (not while airborne in the base version).
Q: jump to the point under the cursor, clamped to the jump range; a landing ring follows the cursor while Q is held and the jump goes on release. One counted key.
Grapple-line variant: Q fires the line at a wall or ledge under the cursor and reels you in; Q again lets go.
Launch-pad variant: Q places the pad; anyone who walks onto it is thrown in the direction they move.
The universal keys work as on every unit.
feedback: A landing ring in the jumper's team colour on the ground a moment before it lands, and a shadow under the arc that grows as it falls.
A take-off sound and burst (jets, legs) that carries some distance, as jump packs do in Halo.
Landing strike: the impact radius is drawn with the landing ring, with a dust burst and knockback on impact.
The cooldown shows on the jumper's HUD and as a small pip over it for enemies close by.
Walls and ledges a jump can clear carry one consistent edge marking, so everyone knows which routes are open.
changes_from_rts: In the RTS the player clicks a spot and the unit lands there perfectly. Here the landing is aimed, clamped to range and placed on valid ground, with a ring enemies can read.
Height is hard to read from a top-down camera, so walls and ledges need marked height classes: low walls can be cleared, high ones can't.
The Sickle's landing can squash infantry, and an instant kill from a landing feels random to the victim; here landings do modest damage and knockback after a visible warning.
Some RTS jumpers are nearly immune in the air (Dawn of War II's squads take little ranged damage airborne); here a jumper stays hittable as a low flier, so a jump is a gamble rather than a dodge.
Cooldowns sit longer than many RTS ones, or jumps are stored as charges, and landing has a short recovery, so a jump can't escape every fight.
Take-off and landing are decided on the server with lag compensation, so a jumper never lands inside a wall on someone else's screen.

team_play.notes: Mostly a personal tool, but it opens fights, scouts high ground, and with the pad variant shares the route with the team; the other team answers it together by covering landing spots.

notes: A jump arc with a landing point is simple, but the map needs height classes for walls and ledges and rules for what a jump can clear.
Landing placement: snap to the nearest valid ground, never inside walls, units or vehicles.
An airborne state that decides which weapons, effects, mines and hazards apply mid-air, counting the jumper as a low flier.
Server authority and lag compensation for take-off and landing positions.
Variants add work: a grapple line needs attach points on surfaces, and a launch pad is a placed object anyone can use.
Escape on demand: a short cooldown makes a unit very hard to pin down; tune the cooldown against the length of a typical fight.
High ground: jumping onto perches nobody else can reach can create spots nobody can answer, so mark which ledges are reachable.
A landing strike on a short cooldown next to a strong weapon can wipe groups; keep the strike modest.
Stored jumps let a unit chain its way out of every trap.
Airborne and grounded must look different from above (shadow, height cue), or players waste shots or miss their window.
The landing spot must show for enemies a moment before the jumper lands.
Players must know which walls and ledges a jump can clear.

variants.name: Vault
variants.summary: A plain jump to a spot within reach over walls, gaps and ledges, with no effect on landing.
variants.seen_in: Command & Conquer 3 Zone Trooper jetpack, Dawn of War Assault Marines

variants.name: Landing strike
variants.summary: The landing hurts enemies in a small circle and knocks them back, more the closer they stand to the centre, after the landing ring has warned them.
variants.seen_in: Red Alert 3 Sickle Flea Jump, Dawn of War II Assault Squad, Overwatch Winston

counters.why: Coming down in a group of soldiers scatters and hurts them.

variants.name: Ledge hop
variants.summary: No key: the unit hops up and down one level of ledge whenever it walks into one, but it can't clear walls or energy barriers.

adds_strengths.why: Hops up and down ledges at will, so it raids and escapes where pursuers must walk round.

adds_weaknesses.why: Only one level at a time and never over walls or barriers, so a closed position still stops it.

variants.name: Stored jumps
variants.summary: Two jumps are stored and refill one at a time, so it can chain them, but an empty stock takes a long time to refill.

variants.name: Hard to hit in the air
variants.summary: While airborne it takes much less ranged damage and ignores suppression, but it can't fire until it lands.
variants.seen_in: Dawn of War II Assault Squad; BattleTech's rule that a 'Mech in mid-jump is tougher to hit

variants.name: Pop-up shot
variants.summary: A short hop straight up from behind cover: while airborne its shots pass over low cover, and it can be hit over that cover too, until it drops back down.
variants.seen_in: MechWarrior Online poptarting with jump jets

variants.name: Grapple line
variants.summary: Fire a line at a wall or ledge and reel yourself up to it; the line can also hurt a soldier it hits, and it misses if nothing is in reach.
variants.seen_in: Battlefield 2042 grapple gun, Battlefield Hardline grappling hook

variants.name: Launch pad
variants.summary: Place a pad that throws anyone who steps on it over walls in the direction they move, teammates and enemies alike; it is loud and can be shot.

adds_strengths.why: Its pad launches the whole team over walls and gaps, not just itself.

adds_weaknesses.why: The pad stays where it was placed, anyone can use it, enemies included, and it can be shot.

variants.name: Crushing drop
variants.summary: A heavy walker jumps and lands right on an enemy walker for a big hit; a miss or a blocked landing hurts its own legs and leaves it stuck in recovery.

counters.why: Landing on top of an enemy walker hits it very hard.

adds_weaknesses.why: A missed or blocked landing damages its own legs and leaves it stranded in recovery.

adds_strengths.why: Clears walls, gaps and ledges that stop others, so it picks its angle of attack and escapes where pursuers must walk round.

adds_weaknesses.why: Each jump is a fixed arc whose landing spot shows a moment early, followed by a short recovery while the key recharges.

counters.why: Jumps onto the high ground and past the cover that snipers rely on.

countered_by.why: Mines and traps on the likely landing spots punish a predictable jump.
A root pins it in place so it can't jump away when its key comes back.

open_questions: Can a jumper be hit by everything that reaches low fliers while airborne, or only at take-off and landing?
Which walls and ledges can a jump clear: every low wall, or only marked ones?
Should a landing do damage at T1 at all, and how much?
One jump on a cooldown, or a stock of two that refills one at a time?

shooter_fit.reason: A proven shooter verb (Overwatch, PlanetSide 2, Battlefield) that opens routes and dives; a top-down camera needs clear wall heights, shadows and landing rings to read it.

review.notes: Re-checked field by field against its sources by the batch r1 checker, which covered all 33 batch patterns; research/r1/checker/checks.json lists every field and verdict. The wrong paths were fixed as the skeptic confirmed (cbe6de8).
